data.body:
**Due:** (your teacher will tell you)

Ice, liquid water, and water vapor are the same substance in different states. Their particles are arranged differently and move differently. Water vapor is invisible.

1. Read **The Dance Floor** — the whole lesson is in that one comparison.
2. Learn the words in the **Glossary**, then win the **Matching** game.
3. Keep the **Three States** chart nearby.
4. Sort the cards in **Solid, Liquid, or Gas?**
5. Practise explaining with **Matter Frames**, then check yourself against the rubric.
6. Take the quiz. Question 3 is the one that catches almost everybody.
7. Lock the ideas in with **Remember the Dance Floor** — study the example aid, then make one your own.
8. Finish with **Investigation: The Disappearing Puddle** — use what you learned on a real problem, and mark every guess as a guess.

One thing to watch for all lesson: nothing is created or destroyed when matter changes state. It only rearranges. ❄️💧☁️

history.title: The Dance Floor
history.data:
## The Dance Floor

Matter is made of **particles** too small to see with our eyes. Ice and liquid water contain the same water particles, but those particles are arranged differently and move differently.

Imagine a dance floor. In a **solid**, the dancers stay near their places and jiggle. A solid's particles vibrate around fixed positions, so the solid keeps its shape. The comparison is a model: real particles are not people, and not every solid has the same arrangement.

In a **liquid**, imagine dancers moving past one another while staying close. A liquid flows and takes the shape of the part of its container that it fills. Pour water carefully from a glass into a bowl: the shape changes, but you have not added or removed water.

In a **gas**, imagine dancers spread throughout a room. Gas particles move in many directions, far apart compared with their size. A gas spreads to fill its container. The particles themselves do not grow when a substance becomes a gas.

Heating transfers **energy** to a substance. It can raise the temperature or cause a change of state. While pure ice melts at its melting point, added energy helps change its arrangement rather than raising its temperature. More heat does not always mean a higher temperature.

Ice **melts** into liquid water. Liquid water can **evaporate** from its surface without boiling. Boiling forms vapor bubbles throughout the liquid. Water vapor can **condense** into droplets when it cools. Liquid water can **freeze** when energy leaves it.

Water vapor is invisible. The white cloud beyond a kettle spout is tiny liquid droplets formed as vapor cools. A short clear gap may separate the spout and visible mist.

Matter does not vanish during these changes. In a closed container, the total mass stays the same when ice melts. Include all the contents when measuring. An open puddle loses water to the surrounding air as invisible vapor: its particles still exist, even when they are no longer in the puddle.

data.title: Remember the Dance Floor
data.instructions: Each card locks in facts from The Dance Floor. Study the example, then make the aid your own and explain how it points back to how particles move.
data.sourceExcerpt: Solids have particles vibrating around fixed positions. Liquid particles move past one another. Gas particles spread throughout a container. In a closed container, total mass stays the same during a state change.

cards.target: How particles are arranged and move in three states
essentialFacts: Solid particles vibrate around fixed positions.
Liquid particles remain close but move past one another.
Gas particles spread throughout a container.
cards.aiExample: Imagine dancers jiggling in their places, moving past close neighbors, or moving throughout a room. These represent a solid, a liquid, and a gas.
cards.mapping: The crowd is a model of arrangement and movement, not a temperature scale or an exact picture of water particles.
cards.scaffoldStarter: Fixed places: ____. Moving past neighbors: ____. Spread through a room: ____.
scaffoldSteps: Describe how each group can move.
Match each group to solid, liquid, or gas.
coachPrompts: How does your model show particles moving even in a solid?
cards.studentPrompt: Describe your own crowd picture for the three states.
cards.reasoningPrompt: How does your picture show that the particles are the same in all three states?

hookFact.text: Ice and liquid water contain the same water particles in different arrangements.

cards.target: The four state changes and which way heat goes
essentialFacts: Adding heat: melting (solid to liquid), then evaporating or boiling (liquid to gas).
Removing heat: condensing (gas to liquid), then freezing (liquid to solid).
Every change can be reversed by sending the heat the other way.
cards.aiExample: Heating can change ice to liquid water and liquid water to vapor. Cooling can change vapor to droplets and liquid water to ice.
cards.mapping: The arrows track changes of state and the direction of energy transfer, not a guarantee that temperature always changes.
scaffoldSteps: Write the three states on three rungs, solid at the bottom.
Label the arrows going up with melt and evaporate.
Label the arrows going down with condense and freeze.
coachPrompts: Which two words belong to cooling, and how will you remember they go together?
cards.studentPrompt: Draw or write your own ladder with the four change words.
cards.reasoningPrompt: How does your ladder show what heat does to the particles?

hookFact.text: The fog on a bathroom mirror is water vapor condensing back into liquid.

cards.target: The big rule: matter changes how it behaves, not how much there is
essentialFacts: The total mass of a closed container and its contents stays the same when ice melts.
A puddle that dries up did not vanish; its particles spread into the air as invisible vapor.
Nothing is created or destroyed when matter changes state.
cards.aiExample: Keep all the matter, let ice rearrange; measure the mass through a change.
cards.mapping: The rhyme pairs the three changes with the one fact that never changes, so saying the changes out loud pulls the rule along with them.
scaffoldSteps: List two or three change words that fit a beat.
End the line with what stays the same: the amount, the mass, the stuff.
Clap it out and fix any word that trips the rhythm.
coachPrompts: Does your rhyme say what stays the same, or only what changes?
cards.studentPrompt: Write your own two-line rhyme for the big rule.
cards.reasoningPrompt: How does your rhyme remind you that the puddle did not disappear?

items.text: In a ____, the particles are ____, which is why it ____.

The puddle disappeared because the water ____ into a ____; it did not vanish.

data.rubric:
| Criteria | 1 — Starting | 3 — Getting There | 5 — Particle Thinker |
|---|---|---|---|
| Particle picture | Describes what it looks like | Says how the particles move in one state | Explains a change of state by what the particles do |
| Matter words | Everyday words only | Uses 1-2 glossary words correctly | Uses 3+ glossary words correctly, including melt, evaporate or condense |
| Nothing created or destroyed | Says the water "went away" | Says it changed state | Says where it went and that the amount of matter stayed the same |

history.title: Matter Check

questions.question: What is the real difference between ice and liquid water?
options: They are made of completely different particles
Ice has more particles packed inside it
How the particles are arranged and move relative to one another
Water has energy and ice has none at all
questions.correctAnswer: How the particles are arranged and move relative to one another

questions.question: Why does a gas fill its whole container while a liquid does not?
options: Gas is lighter than the container
Liquids are attracted to the bottom by magnetism
Gas particles are much larger than liquid particles
Gas particles are far apart and bounce around the entire space
questions.correctAnswer: Gas particles are far apart and bounce around the entire space

questions.question: You see a white cloud above a boiling pot. What is it?
options: Tiny liquid droplets that formed when hot vapor cooled
Pure water vapor, which is naturally cloudy and white
Smoke rising from the hot metal of the pot
Ordinary air being pushed up and out of the pot
questions.correctAnswer: Tiny liquid droplets that formed when hot vapor cooled

questions.question: An ice cube melts completely in a sealed container. What happens to its mass?
options: It gets lighter, because solid ice weighs more than liquid water
It stays exactly the same
It gets heavier because water is denser
The mass disappears along with the ice cube's shape

questions.question: Water droplets appear on the outside of a cold glass on a hot day. What happened?
options: Water leaked out through tiny holes in the glass
The glass melted slightly and dripped
The ice inside evaporated through the glass
Water vapor in the air condensed on the cold surface
questions.correctAnswer: Water vapor in the air condensed on the cold surface

questions.question: A puddle on the sidewalk disappears after a sunny afternoon. Explain where the water went using the word particles.
questions.expectedAnswer: Water particles escape from the liquid surface into the air as invisible water vapor. Energy from the surroundings supports evaporation. The particles still exist in the surrounding air.

questions.question: Use the dance-floor comparison to explain the difference between a solid and a liquid to a younger student.
questions.expectedAnswer: In a solid, dancers jiggle around their places. In a liquid, they stay close but can move past one another. This models why a solid keeps its shape and a liquid flows.

reflections.text: Describe one state change you have seen at home this week.
Which state would you rather be a particle in — solid, liquid, or gas? Explain your choice.

history.meta: 5 MCQ + 2 short answer • Q3 is the steam trap

data.question: Is there a fourth state of matter? 🔥
data.answer: Yes. Plasma contains freely moving electrons and electrically charged particles. Lightning and the Sun contain plasma. This lesson focuses on solid, liquid, and gas.

data.question: Is glass a very slow liquid?
data.answer: A famous claim, and it is basically a myth. Old windows are thicker at the bottom because of how glass used to be made, not because it flowed. Glass at room temperature behaves as a solid.

data.question: Why does ice float when most solids sink in their own liquid? 🧊
data.answer: When water freezes, its molecules form an open arrangement with extra space. Ice is less dense than liquid water, so it floats.

data.question: Can something be two states at once?
data.answer: Yes. A mixture can contain ice and liquid water together. During melting, some water is still solid while some is liquid.

data.question: What is dry ice? ❄️
data.answer: Dry ice is solid carbon dioxide. At ordinary air pressure it changes directly to invisible gas, called sublimation. The visible fog near it is mainly tiny water droplets formed as surrounding moist air cools.

data.question: Does air really weigh something?
data.answer: Yes. Air has mass and occupies space, even though we cannot see it. Scientists can measure its mass; the amount depends on how much air is present.

data.title: The Disappearing Puddle
data.instructions: Plan a fair test that shows where the water in a puddle goes and what makes it go faster. Use the lesson's particle idea to predict, then design a test someone else could repeat.
data.fitReason: Measurements of open and covered trays help students distinguish water leaving a tray from matter ceasing to exist.

brief.context: Two identical trays of water are left on the same windowsill. By the next morning one is nearly empty and the other is still half full. A younger student says the water in the empty tray 'is just gone.' Your class has trays, water, a kitchen scale, a fan, a lamp, and plastic wrap.
brief.audience: A second-grade class that wants to know where the water went
brief.drivingQuestion: Where does the water in a drying tray go, and which one change (heat, moving air, or a cover) makes the most difference in how fast it goes?
brief.seedDirection: Weigh each tray and its contents before and after. Less mass in an open tray shows that matter left the tray; this measurement alone does not show where it went.
lockedLessonFacts: Heating transfers energy and can raise temperature or cause a state change.
Evaporation changes liquid water into invisible water vapor that spreads into the air.
The visible white cloud above boiling water is liquid droplets, not vapor; real vapor cannot be seen.
Nothing is created or destroyed when matter changes state; a puddle that dries up did not vanish.
openQuestions: Does moving air or warmth matter more for this tray?
How do we make the trays a fair comparison, changing only one thing?
If we cover a tray with plastic wrap, where will the water show up?
stakeholders: Your teammates who will repeat the test
criteria: Only one thing changes between the two trays in each test
Water is measured by weight before and after, not guessed
The explanation uses particles and the word evaporate correctly
The result is written so a second grader could follow it
constraints: No boiling water or open flames
Tests must finish within two school days
brief.deliverable: A one-page test plan with a data table (starting weight, ending weight, what changed), your prediction, your result, and a two-sentence explanation for second graders of where the water went.

parallelExample.context: A student investigated whether moving air changes drying rate.
parallelExample.move: She placed two identical equally wet towels side by side under the same light and temperature. A fan blew across only one. She weighed both before and after the same time interval.
parallelExample.whyItHelps: She aimed to change only air movement. Repeated measurements help her compare how much water left each towel.

supports.frameStarter: We think the tray with ____ will lose more water because its particles ____.
frameChoices: Warm the tray with a lamp
Blow air across the tray with a fan
Cover one tray with plastic wrap
Put one tray in a cooler spot
coachPrompts: If both trays change two things at once, what will you be unable to say?
Where did the missing weight go? Point to it in the room.
What might droplets inside a covered tray suggest? What other observations would support your explanation?

data.coachHint: Measure carefully. A decrease in an open tray shows matter left that tray; explain where it went using the particle model.
data.sourceExcerpt: A puddle that dries up did not vanish — its particles spread into the air. Matter changes how it behaves, not how much of it there is.
